---
title: "Our Pipeline"
---

To create the objects that are ultimately returned to users there are a number of steps taken beyond what is contained in the curatedMetagenomicData package – this document is intended to add some clarity and transparency to the process. Roughly, the process is as follows: a study is selected for inclusion, metadata for each sample in the study is manually curated, and raw sequencing data for each sample is acquired (prioritizing ENA for speed, with fallback to NCBI SRA). The raw data is preprocessed and run through our [curatedMetagenomicsNextflow](https://github.com/seandavi/curatedMetagenomicsNextflow) pipeline. This Nextflow pipeline performs quality control, host decontamination, and executes multiple profiling tools (MetaPhlAn, Kraken2, KMA/CARD, and optionally HUMAnN). The processed data for all samples in a study are then combined into matrices for each data type, saved as R objects, and uploaded to ExperimentHub. Finally, these matrices are used to construct `(Tree)SummarizedExperiment` objects on the fly that are returned to users.

# Curation

The curation process takes place on GitHub in the [curatedMetagenomicDataCuration](https://github.com/waldronlab/curatedMetagenomicDataCuration) repository. Sample metadata for every sample included in curatedMetagenomicData is manually curated by humans and checked against a standardized template for accuracy. The process is labor-intensive and information comes from three principal sources: journal articles (and their supplementary materials), metadata included when samples were uploaded to NCBI/ENA, and other publications referring to or augmenting the original journal articles. Not only is explicit information (i.e. tables that enumerate the values of variables for each sample) sought out, but implicit information (e.g. "all the subjects in the study were non-smokers") is also included where it occurs in text. The manually curated sample metadata is continuously updated with the advent of new information (this is common when reanalyses find issues) and these changes propagate from the curation repository to the R package weekly.

# Processing

Raw sequencing reads are processed using our standardized [curatedMetagenomicsNextflow](https://github.com/seandavi/curatedMetagenomicsNextflow) pipeline, which ensures reproducible and scalable execution. The core steps of the processing pipeline include:

1. **Read Acquisition and QC:** Raw FASTQ files are downloaded from ENA or SRA, followed by initial quality control using FastQC.
2. **Preprocessing (Kneaddata):** Reads undergo quality trimming and adapter removal using Trimmomatic (e.g., sliding window quality filtering). Host contamination (e.g., human or mouse) is then removed by aligning reads against reference genomes using Bowtie2.
3. **Taxonomic Profiling:** 
   - **MetaPhlAn:** Host-decontaminated reads are profiled using [MetaPhlAn](https://github.com/biobakery/MetaPhlAn) (version 4+) to generate marker presence, marker abundance, and relative abundance profiles. The pipeline also extracts strain-level markers using StrainPhlAn's `sample2markers.py`.
   - **Kraken2 / Bracken:** (upcoming in cMD4) A complementary read-based whole-community taxonomic profile is generated using Kraken2 and Bracken.
4. **Resistome Profiling:** (upcoming in cMD4) Antimicrobial resistance genes are profiled by aligning reads against the CARD database using KMA.
5. **Functional Profiling:** When enabled, [HUMAnN](https://github.com/biobakery/humann) is run to quantify gene families and pathway abundances (with CPM and relative abundance normalizations).
6. **Rarefaction:** (upcoming in cMD4) The pipeline automatically runs a parallel "rarefied" branch, where reads are downsampled (e.g., to 1 million reads) before profiling, enabling standardized cross-sample comparisons of alpha diversity.

The outputs from the pipeline are uploaded to a cloud storage bucket. These include directories (one for each data type) of TSV files (one for each sample) that serve as the input for the R pipeline.

# R Pipeline

The collection of TSV files are not obviously or immediately useful – there is a pipeline written in R to process these outputs into relevant matrix objects for user consumption. The [curatedMetagenomicDataPipeline](https://github.com/waldronlab/curatedMetagenomicDataPipeline) repository on GitHub details the methods that are used to construct and save the matrices for each study that are uploaded to ExperimentHub. Large data types like `gene_families` are stored as sparse matrices, while others are stored as standard matrix objects. The upload to ExperimentHub is ultimately done using the `aws-cli` with credentials from Bioconductor specific to the curatedMetagenomicData package.

As for why we construct matrix objects: the process of combining the samples into a matrix can take hours even on heavy-duty equipment (many cores, many GB of RAM). This is both the advantage and crux of curatedMetagenomicData – subsetting the matrix takes mere seconds and simple laptops are powerful enough; however, the ability to download many single samples across studies is lost. We accomplish the latter in the R package by matrix subsetting and merging in the `returnSamples()` method. All alternatives considered, this is the optimal trade-off, but we are working towards something more efficient in the future – stay tuned!
